title: Mummified crocodile
Cataloguer: Gayle Gibson | ROM Staff, 1990-2015; ROM Volunteer 2015-Present
fulltext:
Mummified crocodile | Gallery Location | Not on View | Medium | Animal remains; plant | Geography | Undetermined site, Egypt | Date | c. 664-332 BC | Period | 26th-30th Dynasty, Late Period | Dimensions | 27 cm | Object number | 910.169.12 | Cataloguer | Gayle Gibson | ROM Staff, 1990-2015; ROM Volunteer 2015-Present | Collection | Egypt | Department | Art & Culture: Ancient Egypt & Nubia | Description | The Ancient Egyptians mummified millions of animals and birds, but, perhaps because the reason behind this practice was so obvious to them, they never wrote down why they did it.  Though some pets were mummified, most animal mummies were animals raised in temple precincts for eventual sacrifice and mummification.  Specially chosen animals were the avatars of gods, such as the sacred hawk at Edfu or the Apis bull at Memphis.  Most animals, however,  may have been seen rather as heralds who entered the Afterlife grateful to the sponsor who paid for their care and feeding and embalming.  They were very often given as Votive Offerings.
Crocodiles were sacred to the god Sobek, who was seen as soverign of the Nile.  Crocodiles were one of the man-eaters of ancient Egypt, who needed to be appeased.

fulltext: Mummified crocodile | Gallery Location | Galleries of Africa: Egypt | Medium | Animal remains, linen | Geography | Probably al-Fayyūm, Egypt | Date | c. 30 BC-642 AD | Period | Roman Period | Dimensions | 77 cm | Object number | 910.169.2 | Cataloguer | Gayle Gibson | ROM Staff, 1990-2015; ROM Volunteer 2015-Present | Collection | Roman World | Egypt | Department | Art & Culture: Ancient Egypt & Nubia | Description | Crocodile mummies are representative of the powerful god, Sobek.  Crocodiles were admired for their ferocity, but also for their parenting skills. The Greek writer Diodorus Siculus told a story of the first king of united Egypt, Menes, being chased by a pack of wild dogs to the edge of a swamp.  The king was saved by a crocodile, who carried him to safety on his back. The story purports to show the ancient connection between kings and crocodiles; it may be a folk-explanation for the use of the crocodile hieroglyph to write "Ity" - a word for sovereign. | Some crocodiles enjoyed long and well-fed lives in pools at temples as manfiestations of the god; they were mummified after their deaths.  Most mummified crocodiles, however, were very young animals, even hatchlings, who were deliberately killed to be mummified and offered as votives to the god.  Presumably these animals in some way enjoyed an eternal life with (or as) the god. | The elaborate wrappping of this animal is typical of crocodiles mummified during the Roman period in Egypt.

fulltext: Mummified crocodile | Gallery Location | Galleries of Africa: Egypt | Medium | bone & skin | Geography | Egypt | Date | c. 200 BC | Period | Late Period or Ptolemaic Period | Dimensions | 25.5 × 2 × 2 cm | Object number | 910.169.11 | Cataloguer | Gayle Gibson | ROM Staff, 1990-2015; ROM Volunteer 2015-Present | Collection | Egypt | Department | Art & Culture: Ancient Egypt & Nubia | Description | The crocodile, the lion, and the hippo were the three man-killers of Ancient Egypt, the most dangerous animals in the land. Often both male and female forms were honoured as divine, though sometimes with quite different attributes. The divine form of crocodile was called Sobek. | Ancient Egyptians did not have a separate word for animal, nor did they believe that animals were inferior, soul-less beings. They believed that animals also possess a | ba, | that part of the soul which moves and eats and copulates, both in this world and the next. A human being could send a message to a god by ceremonially addressing the | ba | of an animal associated with that deity. The message might be a complaint, a request or a vow; the devotee might also ask for protection from an evil spirit. | While an adult, mummified crocodile might be used as an image of the god, Ancient Egyptians offered small mummified crocodiles, often in coffins, to Sobek as messengers to carry their requests for divine assistance.

Description: The Nile crocodile, known from freshwater habitats in sub-Saharan Africa, along the Nile Basin and Madagascar.  his juvenile specimen is approximately one-fifth of its adult size. As adults, Nile crocodiles become apex predators, feeding on almost anything they encounter, and can reach lengths of up to 5 meters and weigh nearly 800 kg.
